title: Gender differences in associations between digital media use and psychological well‐being: Evidence from three large datasets
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Adolescents spend an increasing amount of time using digital media, but gender differences in their use and in associations with psychological well-being are unclear. METHOD: We drew from three large, representative surveys of 13- to 18-year-old adolescents in the U.S. and UK (total N = 221,096) examining digital media use in hours per day and several measures of psychological well-being separately in each of the three datasets. RESULTS: Adolescent girls spent more time on smartphones, social media, texting, general computer use, and online, and boys spent more time gaming and on electronic devices in general. Associations between moderate or heavy digital media use and low psychological well-being/mental health issues were generally larger for girls than for boys. Light users of digital media were slightly higher in well-being than non-users, with larger differences among boys. Among both genders, heavy users of digital media were often twice as likely as low users to be low in well-being or have mental health issues, including risk factors for suicide. CONCLUSIONS: Associations between heavy digital media use and low psychological well-being are larger for adolescent girls than boys.

claims.text: Adolescent girls spend more time on smartphones, social media, texting, general computer use, and online than adolescent boys.
Adolescent boys spend more time gaming and on electronic devices in general than adolescent girls.
Associations between moderate or heavy digital media use and low psychological well-being or mental health issues are larger for adolescent girls than for boys.
Light users of digital media exhibit slightly higher psychological well-being than non-users.
The positive difference in well-being between light digital media users and non-users is larger among boys than girls.
Heavy users of digital media are often twice as likely as low users to experience low psychological well-being or mental health issues.

limitations.text: Gender differences in digital media use and in associations with psychological well-being were previously unclear.
